t: Brazil was a slave society from the outset: about 35 per cent of all Africans taken in the Atlantic slave trade were sent there, more than ever reached the Thirteen Colonies, and the trade lasted longer than in any other country of the Americas.
Sugar made the colony: from 1600 to 1650 it was 95 per cent of exports, and in the Bahia sugar regions owners found it cheaper to work the enslaved to death over a few years and buy replacements.

The enslaved fled to fortified settlements called quilombos; the largest, the Quilombo dos Palmares under Ganga Zumba and Zumbi, grew to many thousands and held out until Domingos Jorge Velho destroyed it and killed Zumbi in 1695.
dyk: Only two of the fifteen hereditary captaincies into which John III divided Brazil in 1534–1536 prospered: Pernambuco by growing sugar, and São Vicente chiefly by capturing Indigenous people to trade them as slaves.
ev: On 22 April Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet of 13 ships lands at what is now Porto Seguro and takes possession of the land in the name of Manuel I.
John III divides the land into fifteen hereditary captaincies; only Pernambuco and São Vicente prosper.
Tomé de Sousa arrives as first governor-general with the first Jesuits and founds the capital, Salvador, on All Saints Bay.
Estácio de Sá founds Rio de Janeiro in the war against France Antarctique; the last French settlers are expelled in 1567.
The Dutch West India Company holds Recife, Olinda and the sugar coast as Dutch Brazil until it withdraws in 1654.
An army under Domingos Jorge Velho destroys the Quilombo dos Palmares and kills Zumbi.
The capital of the State of Brazil moves from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro, nearer the gold of Minas Gerais.
Prince Regent John and the Portuguese court arrive in Brazil, fleeing Napoleon, and open its ports to friendly nations.

f.founder: Pedro Álvares Cabral, who took possession for Manuel I on 22 April 1500; Tomé de Sousa, the first governor-general, founded the central government in 1549
f.predecessor: The lands of Indigenous peoples such as the Tupinambá and Guaianaz, assigned to Portugal by the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)
f.successor: The Kingdom of Brazil within the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves (1815), then the Empire of Brazil (1822)
